docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Unreleased

This documentation is built from rig main. It describes changes that may not be in any release yet.

docs.title: rig
docs.text:
rig is a small command-line tool for the mechanical parts of a branch-per-task workflow: pushing a task branch, opening and reading pull requests, waiting for CI, keeping tasks, findings and notes, and printing where the work stands. It was built for loops where coding agents run these steps many times a day, but it does not depend on any particular loop.

It exists for two reasons:

  • A narrow push. rig push takes a task id or a branch name and nothing else. It cannot push the default branch, a tag, a refspec or a force push, so it is safe to allow without a prompt.
  • One interface over two forges. The same commands and the same output work on GitHub and GitLab. rig runs gh or glab underneath and uses the login you already have. It stores a token only for Jira, which has no such tool, and then in the OS keychain.
  • Tasks and rules you define. Tasks, findings and notes live in your repository's git directory, outside any branch. A workflow file you write says which states a task passes through and what must be true before each move, and rig refuses a move that breaks it. See docs/workflows.md.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
rig needs Go 1.24 or later, git, and gh (GitHub) or glab (GitLab).

go install github.com/AindriuB/rig/cmd/rig@latest

Release binaries for five platforms, with a SHA256SUMS file and its SHA256SUMS.sig signature, are on the project's GitHub release page. Releases are signed from 0.5.2; earlier releases are not, and rig update will not install them.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
rig update            # install the latest release
rig update --check    # report only; exit 1 when a newer release exists
rig update --to 0.5.2 # install a given release

rig update replaces the running binary with the release binary for your platform. That includes a copy you built with go install: it is replaced by the release binary built from the same tag, not rebuilt from source. It downloads only from the project's GitHub releases, and installs only after the signature, the checksum and a run of the new binary's version all pass. If any of them fails, or the directory is not writable, the installed file is untouched.

A process that is already running keeps the old binary: on Linux and macOS the old file is replaced, not edited, so a running process keeps its inode, and on Windows the old binary is moved to rig.exe.old (removed on a later run). Start rig again to use the new one.

docs.title: Automatic updates
docs.text:
update.auto sets what rig does after a command finishes:

  • off (the default): nothing.
  • notify: when a newer release exists, print one line to stderr.
  • install: install it, and print one line to stderr.

Set it in the global file only (rig config set update.auto notify --global); a repository cannot turn it on. rig checks at most once every 24 hours, and never changes the command's exit code. It does nothing in CI (CI set), when stderr is not a terminal, with --json, for rig update and rig version, and when the check cannot reach GitHub within 2 seconds.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
rig push <task-id|branch> [--worktree <path>]
rig pr view [<pr|branch> | --task <id>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig pr list [--mine] [--head <branch>] [--state open|closed|merged] [--limit <n>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig pr checks [<pr|branch> | --task <id>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig pr open --head <branch> --title <text> [--base <branch>] [--body <text>] [--draft] [--repo <dir>]
rig pr wait <pr-number | --run <run-id>> [--repo <dir>]
rig status [--json]
rig task new --slug <s> --title <text> [--body <text> | --body-file <path>] [--field <name>=<value>]... [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task new --from [<kind>:]<key> [--state <s>] [--slug <s>] [--field <name>=<value>]... [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task show <task> [--findings] [--notes] [--history] [--children] [--format <text|json|markdown> | --json | --markdown] [--repo <dir>]
rig task edit <task> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task list [--state <s>]... [--all] [--parent <task> | --roots | --tree] [--format <text|json|markdown> | --json | --markdown] [--repo <dir>]
rig task parent <task> <parent|none> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task link <task> [<kind>:]<key> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task unlink <task> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task move <task> <state> [--sha <sha>] [--pr <n>] [--reason <text>] [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task set <task> --field <name>=<value>... [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task count <task> <counter> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task start <slug> [--task-file <path>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task finish <task> --sha <sha> [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig task is <task> <state> [--repo <dir>]
rig task log <task> [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig finding add <task> --severity <sev> --summary <text> [--path <p[:line]>] [--key <k>] [--field <name>=<value>]... [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig finding list <task> [--status <s>]... [--blocking] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig finding set <task> <finding> --status <s> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig note add [<task>] --kind <k> --text <text> [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig note list [<task>] [--kind <k>] [--limit <n>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig workflow show [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig workflow validate [<file>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig next [--who agent|human] [--limit <n>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig context <task> [--budget <tokens>] [--format <text|json|markdown> | --json | --markdown] [--repo <dir>]
rig config get <key> [--global|--repo|--local] [--json]
rig config set <key> <value> --global|--repo|--local
rig config unset <key> --global|--repo|--local
rig config list [--global|--repo|--local] [--show-origin] [--json]
rig tracker pull <key> | --query <q> | --label <l> [--children[=<depth>]] [--limit <n>] [--state <s>] [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig tracker refresh [<task> | --all] [--dry-run] [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig tracker report <task> [--status] [--comment pr|state|summary] [--include findings|notes]... [--dry-run] [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig tracker show <key> [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig tracker status [--json] [--repo <dir>]
rig login                                  (the forge, then Jira when tracker.kind is jira)
rig login <service> [--url <site>] [--user <email>] [--token] [--repo] [--store keychain|file]   (github, gitlab or jira; the flags are for jira; --token stores a personal access token, with no user; --pat is the 0.4.0 name and still works)
rig login status [--json]
rig logout <service> [--url <site>] [--repo]   (jira; github and gitlab print the gh/glab command)
rig version
rig update [--check] [--to <version>] [--json]

--actor <name> (alias --role <name>) is accepted by the commands above that write the store, and by no other. It sets the actor recorded on each event the command writes: a label for the audit trail, not authentication. The actor is the flag, else $RIG_ACTOR, else git's user.name, else unknown. The value is trimmed; an empty one, one with a control character, or --actor and --role given with different values is exit 2, with nothing written.

Command What it does Exit codes rig push Pushes one branch to origin. A task id such as 07 resolves to task/07-<slug>. 0 pushed; 1 the push failed; 2 refused, git never ran rig pr view, checks, list Prints pull requests and their CI state in one neutral form. 0; 2 on any error rig pr open Opens a pull request for a branch that is already pushed. It never pushes. 0; 2 on any error rig pr wait Blocks until a pull request's checks, or one CI run, finish. 0 green; 1 red; 2 error or timeout rig status Prints the handoff note, task files, worktrees and open pull requests, then a view of the store: open tasks with their effective states, and open findings. The store view reads only local data and makes no network call. 0; 2 on a usage error rig task, rig finding, rig note Create and read tasks, findings and notes, and move a task between states. rig task is answers "is it in this state?" with its exit code. 0; 1 refused by a workflow gate, nothing written; 2 on any error rig task show --children, rig task list --parent, --roots, --tree Show a task with its children; list the children of one task, the tasks with no parent, or all tasks as a forest. as rig task rig task parent <task> <parent\|none> Sets or clears a task's parent. A missing parent or a cycle is refused. 0; 1 refused, nothing written; 2 on any error rig task new --from [<kind>:]<key> Creates a task linked to a tracker issue and copies the issue's fields into it. If the issue is already linked, prints that task, with a note on stderr. --state must be one of the workflow's intake states. 0; 1 refused (--state); 2 on any error rig task link <task> [<kind>:]<key>, rig task unlink <task> Links an existing task to an issue and refreshes it, or removes the link and keeps the fields. A linked task's owned fields cannot be changed by rig task set or rig task edit. 0; 1 refused (issue already linked; task not linked); 2 on any error rig task start <slug>, rig task finish <task> --sha <sha> start makes a git worktree and branch task/<slug> for a task file and ties the worktree to it. finish merges exactly the verified commit into the default branch and removes the worktree. 0; 1 refused, nothing changed (a merge conflict is aborted); 2 on any error rig tracker pull Creates linked tasks from one issue, a search or a label, and with --children the issue's sub-issues. 0; 1 --state refused; 2 on any error, or if any issue failed rig tracker refresh Re-reads linked issues and overwrites the owned fields of their tasks with the tracker's values. --dry-run writes nothing. 0; 2 on any error, or if any task failed rig tracker report Sends a linked task's progress to its issue: a status from the workflow's tracker.report.status, then a comment (pr, state or summary; findings and notes only with --include). With neither --status nor --comment it sends the status and a state comment. Each send is recorded in a tracker-report event (the status as from, to and the requested asked). A repeat that changes nothing is skipped; --dry-run prints what would be sent. 0; 1 no status mapped for the state, no such transition, or no pull request for --comment pr, with nothing sent; 2 on any other error rig tracker show, rig tracker status Prints one issue; or prints the tracker kind, whether its configuration is trusted, what it supports and whether the login works, and, for Jira, whether the configured project exists. Neither writes. 0; 2 on any error rig workflow Shows the workflow in effect, or checks a workflow file. 0; validate 1 invalid; 2 on any error rig next, rig context List what each open task needs, and print a size-limited brief for one task. They never call the forge. 0; 2 on any error rig config Reads and writes settings in ~/.rig/config.json (--global, --repo) or <repo>/.rig/config.json (--local). rig config set needs a scope. 0; get 1 not set; 2 on any error rig login, rig logout login hands over to gh or glab for GitHub and GitLab, and stores a Jira token in the keychain. rig login status shows where you are logged in, never a token. 0; 1 a login failed; 2 on any error

--format markdown (or --markdown) prints rig task show, rig task list and rig context as Markdown, for people and for agents that read prose; --format json is the same as --json, and --format text is the default. Naming two different formats, or an unknown one, is exit 2.

An unknown flag always exits 2. --json output and the exit codes are a stable contract, described in docs/design.md. The store and the task commands are described in docs/phase-2.md, config and login in docs/phase-2.5.md, and the workflow file format, with a worked example, in docs/workflows.md.

Tasks live in refs/rig/ and .git/rig/ of the clone, so they stay on your machine: rig does not push or fetch them, and a repository looks the same to anyone who does not use rig. With no setup, rig uses a small built-in basic workflow (open, active, done).

docs.title: What rig push will push
docs.text:
A branch is pushed only if all of these hold:

  • it is <prefix>/<name>, and the prefix is in pushPrefixes (by default task and record);
  • it uses only letters, digits and . _ / -;
  • it is not the repository's default branch;
  • it exists locally.

It is pushed to the branch of the same name on origin. There is no option for another remote, a force push or tags.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
rig config holds the newer settings (the forge, the tracker, the workflow); see docs/phase-2.5.md. .claude/rig.json in the repository is optional and still read. Every key has a default.

Key Meaning Default forge github or gitlab detected from the origin host host the forge's host, for a self-hosted instance the origin host pushPrefixes branch prefixes rig push may push ["task", "record"]

pushPrefixes widens what rig push can do without a prompt, so treat the file as yours: do not let an agent edit it unasked.

The keys of rig config (see rig config list) are:

Key Meaning Default forge.kind, forge.host The forge, and its host for a self-hosted instance detected from the origin host push.prefixes Branch prefixes rig push may push. Never from .rig/config.json ["task", "record"] workflow A workflow preset name or an absolute path. Global file only basic tracker.kind local, jira, github, gitlab or exec local (no tracker) tracker.url The tracker's https:// address. A tracked .rig/config.json cannot supply it none tracker.project A Jira project key, owner/name, or group/.../name the origin remote's path (GitHub, GitLab) tracker.command For exec: the program and its arguments. Global file only none tracker.jira.api auto, v2 or v3 auto tracker.jira.epicField The Jira Server or Data Center "Epic Link" field id found by name tracker.jira.acceptanceField The Jira field id that holds acceptance criteria none update.auto off, notify or install: what rig does after a command when a newer release exists. Global file only off worktrees.root Where rig task start puts worktrees: <root>/<repo name>/<slug> .worktrees

worktrees.root is relative to the repository's main checkout, or absolute. A value that comes from the repository's own .rig/config.json (or the default) must be a relative path without a .. element, and after symlinks are resolved the worktree must still be under the checkout; otherwise rig task start stops with an error. Only the global file may point outside the checkout, with an absolute path. tracker.url has a trust rule of its own: see docs/workflows.md.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
go vet ./...

go test ./...

The tests use throwaway git repositories and stub gh and glab programs, so they need no network and no login. The code is in three layers: commands in cmd/rig, the forge interface in internal/forge, and one adapter per forge below it. docs/design.md has the full design and the phases planned next.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
1. Set version in cmd/rig/version.go. A new command, flag or JSON field raises the minor version; a change to an existing one raises the major.
  2. Tag the commit v<version> and push the tag.
  3. The release workflow builds the binaries and drafts a GitHub release.

docs.title: rig: generic actions for agentic workflows
docs.text:
Status: phase 1 was released as 0.1.0. Phases 2 and 2.5 ship together as 0.3.0 and are described in phase-2.md and phase-2.5.md; workflows.md documents the workflow file. Phase 3 (views and trackers) ships as 0.4.0 and 0.5.0: 0.4.0 is built and is described in phase-3.md; rig tracker report is built in 0.5.0. Later phases are outlines, each planned separately before it is built.

Direction. rig provides generic actions (tasks, findings, notes, workflow transitions, push, pull requests, CI waits, context briefs, config, login) that any loop can use, driven by any harness: Claude Code, other agent CLIs, CI or a person. It has no built-in lifecycle: a workflow file defines states, transitions and the gates that guard them. A review loop is one such workflow, owned by the project that runs it. The sections below that describe such a loop are the history of how rig started.

rig is its own tool. It began as a subdirectory of an agent toolkit and moved here with its history in phase 1.5. Its callers use it only through the contract below.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
rig started as the mechanics of an agent review loop: plan → fanout → review → verify → record. In that loop, state and rules lived in prose and shell text:

  • State is markdown the model re-reads. Task state is parsed out of ## Review round N and ## Wave verified — <sha> sections, then confirmed with gh and git on every turn.
  • Rules are enforced by parsing shell. scripts/push-guard.sh decides whether a Bash command is a safe push by matching its text. A regex cannot understand bash: extending the guard to chained commands took four review rounds, each of which found another way to push to main, and was reverted.
  • It is tied to GitHub. gh is called from scripts/ci-wait.sh and from the status, wave, merged and handoff commands.
  • It does not scale past one developer. Sequential task numbers collide, and PLAN.md and HISTORY.md conflict on merge.

rig is a small Go program that owns the mechanical parts: pushing, pull requests, CI waits and status now; tasks, findings and context later. A command that takes typed arguments can refuse a bad push by construction, where a guard has to recognise one in arbitrary shell.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Go, standard library where possible. One static binary, no runtime.
  • Forge adapters only. gh now, glab next. Git is called directly; there is no git abstraction to swap.
  • The forge is auto-detected from the origin remote's host. The layered config (rig config) overrides it, by the scope order rig config get reports (local, repo section, .claude/rig.json, global), then origin detection. A kind from a less specific scope never overrides a host from a more specific one; a host that names no known forge falls back to a less specific kind. Without a home directory forge selection treats the global layer as empty, but rig push still fails closed (exit 2): its policy may live in the global file.
  • rig holds a token only for a service with no CLI of its own. GitHub and GitLab stay with gh and glab: the adapters shell out to them and use whatever login the user already has, and rig login github|gitlab only hands over to gh auth login or glab auth login. For Jira, which has no such tool, rig login jira stores a token, in the OS keychain unless the user explicitly chooses --store file. No config key holds a token or an account; see phase-2.5.md.
  • No built-in workflow. States, transitions, gates, severities and task fields come from a workflow file; rig ships only a small basic one. What rig enforces whatever the workflow says is listed in phase-2.md.
  • Harness-neutral. The CLI with --json and exit codes, and later an MCP server, are the only surfaces. Nothing assumes Claude Code.
  • scripts/push-guard.sh is unchanged. It stays as the backstop for a raw git push. rig push is the allowed route; the guard is not extended.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Three layers. Only adapters know a technology.

./
  cmd/rig/              commands: policy and output
  internal/forge/       port: Forge interface, PullRequest, Check
  internal/store/       port: Store interface (phase 2)
  internal/tracker/     port: Tracker interface (phase 3); adapters in
                        exec/, jira/, github/, gitlab/, fake/
  internal/forge/github adapter: runs `gh … --json`
  internal/forge/gitlab adapter: runs `glab`
  internal/forge/fake   adapter: in memory, for tests
  internal/git/         rev-parse, push, worktree list, merge-tree
  internal/proc/        shell-free, time-limited subprocess
  internal/config/      .claude/rig.json
  1. Commands (cmd/rig) hold policy and output. Text by default, --json for agents. A command never calls gh, glab or a store backend directly; it calls a port.
  2. Ports (internal/forge, internal/store) are interfaces in neutral types. Nothing in a port names GitHub or GitLab.
  3. Adapters implement a port for one technology. They translate that tool's JSON and vocabulary into the neutral types.

Supporting packages:

  • internal/proc runs a subprocess from an argument vector with a deadline. It never builds a shell string, and when the deadline passes or the context is cancelled it kills the whole process tree, not just the child: the process group on Unix, a Job Object on Windows. One narrow race remains on Windows: a descendant spawned between Start and the job assignment is not in the job and is not killed. A run that succeeds leaves its descendants running, on every platform.
  • internal/git wraps the handful of git calls rig needs.
  • internal/config reads the layered config (rig config); .claude/rig.json is still honoured, and the forge and the push prefixes come from it:
Key Meaning Default forge github or gitlab detected from the origin host host forge host, for self-hosted instances the origin host pushPrefixes branch prefixes rig push may push ["task", "record"]

Install with go install github.com/AindriuB/rig/cmd/rig@<tag>. A caller that installs rig for its users can pin a tag and check rig version against the minimum it needs.

docs.title: The contract between rig and its callers
docs.text:
A caller talks to rig only through its commands, their exit codes and their --json output. It never imports rig's code or reads its files, and rig never reads the caller's. That is what lets rig live in another repository and be versioned on its own.

rig version prints a semantic version (0.1.0 for phase 1, 0.3.0 with phases 2 and 2.5, 0.4.0 with the first part of phase 3) and exits 0. A new command, flag or JSON field raises the minor version. A change to anything in the tables below raises the major version.

Stable commands and exit codes

Command Exit codes rig version 0 rig update [--check] [--to <version>] [--json] 0 updated, or already current (with --check: no newer release, or the target is before 0.5.2); 1 refused (the latest release is older than the running rig, --to names a version before 0.5.2 or one that is not a version, or the binary's directory is not writable, or another update is in progress), or with --check a newer release exists; 2 a usage error (an extra argument, an unknown flag, or --to with no value), a network error, a failed check, or with --check a --to that is not a version rig push <task-id\|branch> [--worktree <path>] 0 pushed; 1 git ran and the push failed; 2 refused, git push never started rig pr view [<pr\|branch> \| --task <id>] [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error, including no such pull request rig pr checks [<pr\|branch> \| --task <id>] [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error rig pr list [--mine] [--head <branch>] [--state open\|closed\|merged] [--limit <n>] [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error rig pr open --head <branch> --title <text> [--base <branch>] [--body <text>] [--draft] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error rig pr wait <pr-number \| --run <run-id>> [--repo <dir>] 0 green; 1 red; 2 error or timeout rig status [--json] 0; 2 on a usage error rig task new --slug <s> --title <text> [--body <text> \| --body-file <path>] [--field <name>=<value>]… [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error rig task new --from [<kind>:]<key> [--state <s>] [--slug <s>] [--field <name>=<value>]… [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0, also when the issue is already linked (the existing task is printed and a line goes to stderr); 1 --state is not an intake state, nothing written; 2 on any other error, including no usable tracker and a --field the tracker owns rig task show <task> [--findings] [--notes] [--history] [--children] [--format <text\|json\|markdown> \| --json \| --markdown] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error, including two different formats rig task edit <task> [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0 saved, or nothing changed; 1 a field changed underneath the edit, or the edit changes a field the linked tracker owns, nothing written; 2 on any error, including no terminal and no $VISUAL/$EDITOR, or a file that does not parse rig task list [--state <s>]… [--all] [--parent <task> \| --roots \| --tree] [--format <text\|json\|markdown> \| --json \| --markdown] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error, and at the end if any task failed (the others are still refreshed) rig tracker report <task> [--status] [--comment pr\|state\|summary] [--include findings\|notes]… [--dry-run] [--actor <name>] [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0, also when an earlier report already sent the same (skipped); 1 the task's state has no tracker.report.status entry, the tracker has no transition to that status, or --comment pr and the task has no pull request, with nothing sent; 2 on any other error, including no tracker, an unlinked task, and a comment that failed after the status was sent (the status is recorded) rig tracker show <key> [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0; 2 on any error rig tracker status [--json] [--repo <dir>] 0, also when the login does not work (it says so); 2 on any other error rig login 0; 1 a login failed; 2 on any error rig login github\|gitlab\|jira [--url <site>] [--user <email>] [--token] [--repo] [--store keychain\|file] 0; 1 the login failed or Jira rejected the token, nothing stored; 2 on any error rig login status [--json] 0; 2 on any error rig logout jira [--url <site>] [--repo] 0, also when already logged out; 2 on any error, including a store that could not be checked when the entry was found nowhere rig logout github\|gitlab 2: prints the gh/glab command that does it

rig update --json prints one object: {current, target, action, path, check?}. action is updated, up-to-date, available, refused or failed; check is signature, checksum or version and is present only when that check failed. Without --json the one-line message is printed.

Self-update. rig update takes releases from one fixed source, the AindriuB/rig releases on the GitHub API. No flag, environment variable or config key changes it. Every request, and every redirect, must be https to api.github.com, github.com, objects.githubusercontent.com or release-assets.githubusercontent.com on the default port, or rig refuses it. Drafts and prereleases are never installed. rig downloads SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.sig and the platform binary, then verifies in this order: the Ed25519 signature (a raw 64-byte .sig) over SHA256SUMS against the keys built into rig; the binary's SHA-256 against its SHA256SUMS line; and the staged binary's rig version, which must print the target version. Only then is the file replaced. The embedded keys are a list, so a key can be rotated.

update.auto (off, notify, install; default off) is read from the global config only. After a command returns, rig checks for a release at most every 24 h (2 s timeout) and prints one stderr line. It is silent in CI, when stderr is not a terminal, with machine output (--json or --format json) and offline, and never changes the exit code.

An update takes a lock on a file beside the binary, .<binary name>.update.lock in the binary's directory. rig update and the automatic install take the same lock. A second rig update is refused with another update of <binary> is in progress and exit 1; the automatic install skips silently, with no stderr line and no change to the exit code. The file is never deleted; the kernel drops the lock when its holder exits.

An unknown flag is always exit 2: rig never ignores an argument it does not understand. In the phase-2 commands, exit 1 means refused by a gate or the workflow with nothing written, and exit 2 covers usage errors, an unknown or ambiguous task, a bad workflow file, and store or git errors. The commands' flags and behaviour are described in phase-2.md and phase-2.5.md, and the workflow file in workflows.md. RIG_ACTOR names who acted and RIG_WORKFLOW the workflow to use. The commands that write the store (task new, edit, move, set, count, parent, link, unlink; finding add, set; note add; tracker pull, refresh, report) also take --actor <name>, or its alias --role <name>, which beats RIG_ACTOR and git's user.name for the actor stamped on the events; an empty or control-character value, or the two flags with different values, is exit 2 with nothing written, and every other command rejects them as unknown options (exit 2); RIG_JIRA_TOKEN overrides a stored Jira token at use time.

Stable text output

  • rig pr wait, green: exactly one line, CI green: PR #<n> or CI green: run <id>. Red: CI red: … first, then the failed names, then at most 40 log lines after --- log tail ---. Errors go to stderr with the prefix ci-wait:.
  • rig pr list, and the pull request lines of rig status: #<n> <ci> <head> <title, at most 50 characters>, then conflict and draft when they apply.
  • rig push, on success: pushed <branch> to origin.
  • rig task start, on success, exactly four lines, with these paddings:
WORKTREE: <worktree path>
BRANCH:   task/<slug>
BASE:     <base branch> @ <short sha> (<local|origin/<base branch>>)
OWNS:     enforced from <task file path>

The base branch is origin's default branch, else main, master, trunk or develop, else the current branch. The task starts from the newer of local <base> and origin/<base>, and BASE names the one used: local or origin/<base>. When the two have diverged, neither contains the other, the task starts from local <base> and rig prints rig: local <base> and origin/<base> have diverged: started from local <base> on stderr. At a detached HEAD with no default or current branch the task starts from HEAD: BASE reads HEAD @ <short sha> (HEAD), with no local or origin comparison. The worktree is <worktrees.root>/<repository directory name>/<slug>. - rig task finish, on success: MERGED: <branch> @ <short sha> -> <base>, then REMOVED: <worktree>, or KEPT: <worktree> (<reason>) when the worktree could not be removed or the branch moved during the merge (its later commits are not merged, and the branch is kept).

The kit-task marker. rig task start writes the file kit-task in the new worktree's own git directory (git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir there), where git never commits it. A caller that guards file ownership (the kit's owns-guard) reads it to find the task file. Its contract: one line, the path of the task file with forward slashes even on Windows, ending in a single LF, with no byte order mark. The path is absolute: rig finds the file in docs/plan/tasks of the main checkout or its enclosing workspace repository, or resolves --task-file against the working directory. If the file cannot be written, rig task start removes what it made and exits 2, so a worktree is never left without its marker.

Stable JSON fields

A pull request, from rig pr view --json and each element of rig pr list --json:

Field Value number integer url, title, head, headSha, base strings state open, closed or merged draft boolean mergeable mergeable, conflicting or unknown mergeSha the merge commit; present only once merged ci red, running, green or none checks array of {name, state, url}; state is pass, fail, cancel, pending or skipped

rig pr checks --json is {number, ci, checks} with the same meanings.

rig status --json is {handoff, tasks, worktrees, prs, prsError}: handoff is {written, lines} or absent; tasks is an array of task file names without .md; each worktree is {path, branch, ahead, dirty}; prs holds pull requests as above; prsError is present when the forge could not be reached, and the rest of the output is still valid. It also has store, the view of the local store, which needs no network: {tasks, findings, error?}. tasks are the tasks not in a final state, in the order a task moves through the workflow. Each is {id, short, slug, title, state, parent?, external?}, where state is the effective state, parent is the parent's short id and external is {kind, key}; findings is {open, byTask}, with byTask mapping a task's short id to its open findings. error is set, and tasks empty, when the store could not be read.

rig task start --json is {worktree, branch, base, baseSha, taskFile}. rig task finish --json is {merged: {branch, sha, base}, kept?: {worktree, reason}, removed?}.

Task JSON. The task printed by rig task show --json, rig task list --json and the other task commands gains parent (a task id; absent when there is none) and external (absent when the task is not linked):

external field Value kind, key the tracker kind (jira, github, gitlab or exec) and the issue key host, project, url, type strings, each left out when empty; type is the tracker's own level label (epic, Sub-task) owned the rig fields the tracker owns syncedAt, rev when the task was last synced, and the tracker's revision of the issue then drift the owned fields whose local value differs from the last snapshot; [] when none

rig task show --children --json is the task with a children array of tasks.

Tracker JSON.

  • rig tracker pull --json is {items, skipped}; an item is {task, key, existing, parent, warnings}, where task is a task as above and parent is the short id of its parent task, or "".
  • rig tracker refresh --json is {tasks}; an entry is {task, key, status, changed, replaced, error?, warnings?}. status is unchanged, updated, gone or error; changed lists the fields that changed; replaced is a list of {field, lost} for each local edit the refresh overwrote.
  • rig tracker report --json is {task, key, status, comment, skipped?, dryRun?, warnings?}; status is {from, to} and comment is {kind, id}, each null when that part was not sent. With --dry-run nothing is sent: status has only to, and comment has no id but a body.
  • rig tracker show --json is the issue: {key, url, title, description, acceptance, priority, assignee, labels, type, status, parent, rev}.
  • rig tracker status --json is {kind, trusted, capabilities, login}; capabilities is {parent, children, types, search, comment, setStatus, levels} or null, and login is {ok, error?}. For a tracker that can check its configured project (Jira) there is also project, {key, exists, empty}, and the text output gains project: RIG ok, project: RIG not found or project: RIG ok (no issues yet); a missing project does not change the exit code. When the check fails with an error, project is {error} and the text output says project: not checked: <error>.

Tracker report. rig tracker report sends a task's progress to the issue it is linked to (the task must be linked to an issue of the configured tracker, else exit 2). With neither --status nor --comment it is --status --comment state.

  • The status is the workflow's tracker.report.status entry for the task's effective state, sent with the tracker's set-status call. It is sent before the comment, so a refusal means nothing has left the machine. A tracker that cannot set a status (or cannot comment) gives a warning and the other part is still sent; an unsupported status is dropped before the skip check, so a repeat whose other part is skipped reports skipped.
  • The comment is one of three fixed templates, and nothing else of the task (title, body, fields) is ever sent:
  • pr: rig: pull request for task <short>: <url>. The URL comes from the forge, by the task's recorded pull request number.
  • state: rig: task <short> is now in state <state>.
  • summary: the state line, then Counters: <name>=<n>, ... (names sorted; left out when the task has none), then Pull request: <url> (left out when the task has none). If the forge read fails, the comment is sent without the Pull request: line and the run warns.
  • --include findings appends a blank line, Open findings: and one - <short> <severity> <summary> line per open finding (nothing when there are none). --include notes appends a blank line, Notes: and one - <kind>: <text> line per note, oldest first. Line breaks inside a summary or note are folded to a space.
  • Each real run that sends something writes one tracker-report event {kind, key, status?: {from, to, asked?}, comment?: {kind, id, digest}, at}, recording only what was sent; digest is the hex SHA-256 of the comment body, and the body itself is not stored. asked is the status name the report requested (to is the one the tracker reached, which may be spelled differently, as GitLab's open becomes opened). An older rig skips the kind.
  • A part is skipped when the latest earlier report for the same issue, written since the task's latest link event, sent the same thing: the status when the requested name equals its last sent asked or to (case and surrounding spaces ignored), the comment when the latest comment of the same kind has the same digest. Two report runs at once can both send: there is no lock. When every requested part is skipped nothing is sent, no event is written, and the output says skipped ("skipped": true in JSON). skipped means the repeat check dropped a part: when the tracker's capabilities alone empty the request, the run exits 0 with the warnings and the normal (or dry-run) line, and skipped is false.
  • --dry-run calls no tracker method that writes, and writes nothing; it prints status: <name> and comment (<kind>): followed by the exact body a real run would send, with the same skip rules and warnings applied (a tracker that cannot set a status or comment, or whose capabilities cannot be read).
  • It never writes planning fields. A comment that fails after the status was sent leaves the status recorded and exits 2; the next run sends the comment.

Markdown format. --format markdown (alias --markdown) is stable like JSON: sections and fields are only added; removing or reordering one is a major change. --format json is the alias of --json. Two different formats, or an unknown one, are exit 2. Text output stays free-form. Every Markdown output is UTF-8 with LF line endings, one trailing newline, no ANSI codes, no wrapping, and times in RFC 3339 UTC. A field with no value is left out, and a single-line value has its line breaks turned into one space.

  • rig task show: # <title>, then a bullet block with these labels in this order, each only when it has a value: id, slug, state, recorded state, branch, pr, head, reason, parent, external, created, updated. Then H2 sections in this order: Body, Fields, Counters, Findings (with --findings), Notes (--notes), History (--history), Children (--children). Body, Fields and Counters are left out when empty; a requested section with nothing in it prints none. Body is a blockquote: line endings become LF and every line starts with > (an empty line is >). So a task body, which may come from a tracker, cannot open a heading, a fence or an HTML block of its own. Fields and Counters are - name: value lines sorted by name. A finding is - <short> [<severity>] <status>: <summary> (<path>); a note is - <time> [<kind>] <text>.
  • rig task list: # Tasks, then a bullet per task, - <short> [<state>] <title> (<slug>), followed by — <key> for a linked task and ← <parent short> for a task with a parent. No tasks prints none. --tree indents each child under its parent in place of the ←.
  • rig context: H2 sections named as the JSON sections[].name (Header, Body, Findings, Paths, Overlap, History, Commits); a section the budget hid is left out. Body is a blockquote as above and the others are - bullets. An omitted count is the line _… <n> more_. The Header has parent: and external: rows for a task that has them. The budget is counted against the Markdown's own bytes; text and JSON are counted as before.

docs.title: What rig push does and does not guarantee
docs.text:
Any command line that starts rig push can only make a non-forced push of one local branch named <prefix>/<name> to the branch of the same name on origin. It cannot name main or any bare branch, a tag, a refspec, another remote, or a force or delete option. Exit 2 means git push never started.

Two things sit outside that guarantee.

  • .claude/rig.json is the user's file. Its pushPrefixes decide which prefixes count, so whoever can write it can widen the pushes: to release/x, say, though still never to a bare branch, a tag or a force. In a bare layout the worktree's own files apply, as for rig config. An agent must not edit it. The project settings template makes any Edit or Write of .claude/rig.json, in the project or in a worktree below it, and any shell command that names rig.json, ask first (tests/rig-settings.bats pins those rules). A permission rule matches text, so this is a barrier, not a proof: a shell command can build the file name without spelling it, and two commands the template already allows can write and run a file (git log --output=<path> and rg --pre <program>). Narrowing those allow rules is a separate change.
  • Git's own configuration is not constrained. A pre-push hook, or remote.origin.receivepack, runs whatever it says during any push, and an agent can set either with git config. rig push runs the repository's hooks like any push does, so it does not close this. The raw git push origin task/<name> form the push guard allows has the same limit. Closing it would mean pushing with hooks disabled, which would also disable the hooks a project relies on; that trade has not been made.

docs.title: The forge port
docs.text:
type Forge interface {
    ViewPR(ctx context.Context, ref string) (PullRequest, error)
    ListPRs(ctx context.Context, opts ListOptions) ([]PullRequest, error)
    CreatePR(ctx context.Context, in CreatePRInput) (PullRequest, error)
    Checks(ctx context.Context, pr int) ([]Check, error)
    WaitChecks(ctx context.Context, target WaitTarget) (WaitResult, error)
    FailedLogs(ctx context.Context, target WaitTarget, failed []Check) ([]LogLine, error)
}

type PullRequest struct {
    Number    int
    URL       string
    Title     string
    State     PRState   // open | closed | merged
    Draft     bool
    Head      string    // head branch
    HeadSHA   string
    Base      string
    Mergeable Mergeable // mergeable | conflicting | unknown
    Checks    []Check
}

type Check struct {
    Name  string
    State CheckState // pass | fail | cancel | pending | skipped
    URL   string
}

WaitTarget is a pull request number or a CI run id. Later phases add Merge, Comment and Reviews.

A pull request's overall CI state is derived from its checks in one place, in the port, so both adapters report it the same way: red if any check failed or was cancelled, else running if any is pending, else green if there is at least one check, else none.

docs.title: Phase 1 commands
docs.text:
Command What it does Exit codes rig push <task-id\|branch> [--worktree <path>] Pushes one loop branch to origin 0 pushed, 1 rejected by the remote, 2 refused rig pr view\|list\|checks Prints neutral output from the forge 0, 2 on error rig pr open --head <branch> … Opens a pull request. Never pushes, and takes its body only from --body, never from a file 0, 2 on error rig pr wait <pr> or --run <id> Blocks until CI finishes 0 green, 1 red, 2 error or timeout rig status [--json] The session brief, worktrees and one line per open PR 0

rig push is the security-relevant command. It resolves a task id to its branch (task/<id>-<slug>, the slug taken from docs/plan/tasks/<id>-*.md, the same lookup as derive_slug in scripts/_wt-common.sh). It then refuses, with exit 2 and without running git, anything that is not a plain branch name under a configured prefix: a refspec (a:b), a + prefix, a .. segment, a tag, any force or delete flag, and any unknown flag. What remains is run as git -C <worktree> push -u origin <branch>:<branch> — an argument vector, so there is nothing for a shell to reinterpret.

rig pr wait keeps the contract of scripts/ci-wait.sh, so callers do not change: the same exit codes, CI green: PR #N as the only line when green, the failed checks and a 40-line log tail when red, and CI_WAIT_TIMEOUT (seconds, default 1800). ci-wait.sh becomes a wrapper that execs rig pr wait.

rig status prints one line per open pull request in the format commands/status.md already uses: #N red|running|green|none branch title [conflict] [draft].

Phase 1 is read-only on documents. State still comes from the existing docs/plan files, git and the forge.

docs.title: The store and workflows (phase 2)
docs.text:
A store holds work in progress outside the code tree: one append-only event log per task under refs/rig/tasks/<ULID>, local to the clone unless the user opts in to sharing it. A task's state is a fold over its events. Which states exist, which transitions are allowed and which gates guard them come from a workflow file, not from rig. Tasks, findings and notes carry typed fields the workflow declares. phase-2.md has the format, the commands and the extension points.

The state machine this section used to define (planned → implementing → reviewed → verified@sha → pr_open → ci_green → ready → merged) is now an example workflow file, shown in phase-2.md as the worked example.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
Phase What it delivers 0 This document, and a baseline of permission prompts and tokens per task 1 rig push, rig pr, rig status, rig version; the github and gitlab adapters 1.5 cli/ moves to its own repository, AindriuB/rig, with its history 2 Shipped in 0.3.0. Generic core: the store port and git-ref backend, workflow files with gates and hooks, rig task, rig finding, rig note, rig workflow, rig next, rig context. An example review loop is a test fixture, not built in 2.5 Shipped in 0.3.0. rig config (global, per-repo and local scopes; forge and tracker settings) and rig login/rig logout with keychain-held tokens 3 Views and trackers, see phase-3.md. 0.4.0 is built: --format markdown for task show, task list and context; task parent and external links (task parent, link, unlink, list --parent\|--roots\|--tree, show --children); a tracker port with github, gitlab, jira and exec adapters; rig task new --from, rig tracker pull, refresh, show and status; branch stamping with {key}; the store view in rig status; rig task start and finish with worktrees.root. 0.5.0: rig tracker report 3.5 Self-update, see phase-3.5.md. 0.5.2: signed releases, rig update, update.auto 4 Team scale: opt-in rig sync of the store, rig claim, retention and rig gc, a search index rebuilt from refs 5 Metrics from event logs, for any workflow: time in each state, counter values, stop reasons, findings by path 6 An MCP server over the same core; each workflow transition becomes a typed tool Later, unscheduled HTML views and templates; an importer for docs/plan task files as a program the user runs. Tracker intake in phase 3 covers most of the importer's use 1.0 Phase 1's compatibility parts (.claude/rig.json, claude-handoff.md and docs/plan/tasks reads, default push prefixes) move behind config or are dropped, as a major change

README, architecture, conventions, release notes and ADRs stay in the tree throughout. Plans, tasks, findings and history are what move into the store, for the projects that choose to use it.

docs.title: Version bump
docs.text:
• File: cmd/rig/version.go — set version to <version>.
  • Commit: release: <version> on a task/release-<version> branch; PR to main.
  • Wait: CI ci.yml green on the PR, then merge.
  • Skip when go run ./cmd/rig version on main already prints <version>.

docs.title: Tag
docs.text:
• git tag -a v<version> -m "<version>" on main's head, then git push origin v<version>.
  • release.yml refuses a tag that does not match rig version.

docs.text: Target Triggered by Workflow Secret it needs GitHub release (draft, 5 binaries + SHA256SUMS + SHA256SUMS.sig) tag push release.yml RIG_SIGNING_KEY (Ed25519 seed, base64; make with go run ./tools/rigsign keygen <dir>) GitHub release published gh release edit v<version> --draft=false --latest none (manual) none

docs.text:
• gh release view v<version> --json isDraft,assets --jq '.isDraft, [.assets[].name]' prints false and rig-{linux-amd64,linux-arm64,darwin-amd64,darwin-arm64,windows-amd64.exe}, SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.sig.
  • go install github.com/AindriuB/rig/cmd/rig@v<version> in a temp GOBIN, then rig version prints <version>.

docs.title: If a step fails
docs.text: • Do not delete or move a pushed tag. Fix forward with <version+patch>.

docs.title: Writing a workflow
docs.text: A workflow tells rig what states a task moves through, which moves are allowed, and what must be true before each move. rig has no lifecycle of its own: the rules live in a JSON file you choose. This page is the reference for that file. phase-2.md explains why the store and workflows exist; this page explains how to write one.

docs.title: Choosing the workflow rig uses
docs.text:
rig loads one workflow per command, from the first of these that is set:

  1. RIG_WORKFLOW, a preset name or an absolute path to a file.
  2. The workflow config key (a preset name or an absolute path). It is read only from the global file, ~/.rig/config.json, and rig config set refuses it: you edit the file by hand.
  3. The built-in preset basic.

A relative path is refused. rig never looks for a workflow inside a repository, so cloning a repository never makes rig run its programs.

rig workflow show prints the workflow in effect and where it came from. rig workflow validate [<file>] checks a file, or the one in effect, and reports any task that is in a state the workflow does not have. It exits 0 when valid, 1 when invalid and 2 on an error.

docs.title: The basic preset
docs.text:
open -> active -> done        any -> stopped        stopped -> (the state before)

States are open (action start), active (action finish), done (final) and stopped (action decide, for a human). Moving to stopped needs a reason. There are no gates. Findings have two severities, blocking and info. Use rig workflow show --json to see the exact file.

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
A workflow is one JSON object. rig refuses a key it does not know, so a typo is an error and not a silent no-op.

Key Meaning name, version A label and a positive integer. A task records both when it is created. initial The state a new task starts in. branch Branch name template; {short}, {slug}, {id} and {key} are replaced. Optional. A task made from an issue (rig task new --from, rig tracker pull) has its branch stamped at creation, but only when the workflow has a branch template (with none, nothing is stamped), with {key} as the issue's key, lowercased, with every run of characters outside a-z, 0-9 and - turned into one -; a later change to the template or the issue does not rename it. Other tasks derive the branch from the template whenever it is read, and there {key} is the task's short id, even after rig task link, so linking never renames a branch. 0.3.0 cannot load a file whose template uses {key}. states An object: state name to {action, who, final, shaBound}, all optional. onNewCommit The state a sha-bound task counts as in when its branch has moved on. Needed if any state is sha-bound. transitions The allowed moves, in order (see below). fields Typed fields on tasks. findings {severities: [...], fields: {...}}. counters Names of counters a task can carry. hooks Programs to run after a move. tracker How issues from a tracker become tasks. Optional. See "Linking tasks to a tracker": 0.3.0 cannot load a file that has this key.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
• action is a label that rig next prints for a task in this state, such as review or merge. rig attaches no meaning to it.
  • who is agent (the default) or human. rig next --who human lists the tasks waiting on a person.
  • final: true means no transition leaves the state, and rig task list hides tasks in it unless you pass --all. A final state cannot be sha-bound.
  • shaBound: true ties a task to the commit it was moved in at. When the task's branch head is no longer that commit, the task's effective state is onNewCommit. This is worked out when the task is read; nothing is written. onNewCommit itself must be neither final nor sha-bound.

State names may not be empty, *, or start with $.

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text:
{ "from": ["a", "b"], "to": "c", "takes": "sha", "count": "rounds", "gates": [ ... ] }
  • from is a state, a list of states, or * for every non-final state other than the target. to is a state, or $previous.
  • $previous means the state the task was in before its latest move. A task that has never moved has none, and the move is refused. rig next shows such a move as blocked by previous.
  • takes names an argument the move records: sha (--sha), pr (--pr) or reason (--reason). A move that takes one refuses to run without it.
  • count adds one to the named counter when the move is written.
  • A move into a sha-bound state that takes no sha inherits the sha of the sha-bound state it came from, so verified -> pr_open carries verified's sha. Otherwise it records none and the state keeps the sha it was last entered at.
  • gates are checked in order before anything is written. Every gate is evaluated and the move happens only if all pass. A refusal is exit 1 and writes nothing. There is no --force: to get past a gate, change the file.

Routes must be unique. After from lists and * are expanded, no two transitions may take the same state to the same target, and one transition may not name a route twice. So {"from": "*", "to": "X"} beside {"from": "a", "to": "X"} is refused, because * already covers a. rig workflow validate reports each clash as route a -> X is also taken by transitions[N]. To give one state different rules from the rest, list the other states explicitly instead of using *.

Validation also requires that every transition names declared states, that no transition leaves a final state, and that every state can be reached from initial. Each problem is reported with its JSON path, for example transitions[3].gates[0].shaIsHead.

docs.title: Gates
docs.text:
A gate is an object with one key, the gate's name.

Gate Passes when {"noOpenFindings": {"severity": ["P1", "P2"]}} no finding with one of those severities is open. Each severity must be declared in findings.severities. {"shaIsHead": true} the sha the move was given is the branch head. The move must take sha. {"shaIs": "<state>"} the sha the move was given is the one recorded when the task entered <state>. The move must take sha. {"dependsIn": ["merged"]} every task named in the depends field is in one of those states. The workflow must declare a depends field of type tasks. A dependency in a sha-bound state is judged by its effective state. {"fieldSet": "<field>"} the field has a value. title and body count as fields. {"counterBelow": {"counter": "rounds", "max": 4}} the counter is below max. max is at least 1. {"command": ["program", "arg", "{short}"]} the program exits 0.

A command gate gets the task as JSON on standard input and has 30 seconds. rig next never runs one: it reports the move's ok as null and the gate as "ok": null, meaning "not run". Only rig task move runs them.

docs.title: Fields, severities and counters
docs.text:
Task fields have a type: string, text, int, bool, list, enum (with values), paths (file globs) or tasks (task references). title and body are built in and cannot be declared. Two flags change how a field is used:

  • context: true prints the field in the fixed part of rig context.
  • owns: true marks the one paths field rig context uses to find the task's files. At most one task field may carry it.

findings.fields are the extra fields a finding takes, such as a route enum. They cannot carry owns. A finding's severity must be one of findings.severities; NOTE or any severity no noOpenFindings gate names never blocks anything.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
{ "on": "enter:stopped", "run": ["notify-user", "{short}", "{reason}"] }

on is enter:<state>, leave:<state> or transition. Hooks run, in file order, after a move has been written. A hook gets {event, task} as JSON on standard input and has 30 seconds. A hook that fails is reported on standard error, and in hookErrors with --json, but it never undoes the move. Something that must be able to refuse a move is a command gate, not a hook.

docs.title: Arguments and placeholders
docs.text: command gates and hooks are argument vectors. rig runs the program directly and never through a shell. An argument that is exactly {short}, {id}, {slug}, {state}, {reason} or {sha} is replaced by that value, and the value stays one argument whatever it contains, spaces and ; included. A placeholder inside longer text, such as --to={state}, is refused by validation. In a hook {state} is the state entered; in a gate it is the state the move leaves.

docs.title: Linking tasks to a tracker
docs.text: A tracker is an issue tracker: Jira, GitHub issues, GitLab issues, or any other that you reach through a program of your own (exec). A task can be linked to one issue. The tracker then owns the task's planning fields, such as its title and description, and rig owns everything about the work itself: state, findings, notes, counters, shas, branch and pull request. Nothing is sent back to the tracker in 0.4.0. rig tracker pull, rig task new --from and rig task link are the commands that use this; see the README for the list.

docs.title: The tracker key
docs.text:
The optional top-level tracker key says how an issue maps to a task. Like the rest of the workflow file, it comes from the global file, so a cloned repository cannot change it.

"tracker": {
  "intake": { "states": ["design", "ready"] },
  "map": {
    "title": "title", "body": "description", "acceptance": "acceptance",
    "priority": "priority", "assignee": "assignee",
    "labels": "labels", "type": "type"
  },
  "report": { "status": { "review": "In Review", "done": "Done" } }
}
  • intake.states lists the states a task may be created in from an issue. The default is the workflow's initial state alone. --state outside the list is refused (exit 1). A listed state must be declared and must not be final.
  • map goes from a rig field to one attribute of the issue. The attributes are title, description, acceptance, priority, assignee, labels and type. The mapped fields are the owned fields: the tracker supplies them, and rig task set and rig task edit refuse to change them on a linked task (exit 1). A key of map is a field the workflow declares, or title, or body. An owned field is not owns: true. labels and acceptance need a list field; every other attribute needs a string or text field. Each attribute is mapped from at most one field. With no map, the owned fields are title and body.
  • report.status goes from a rig state to the name of a tracker status. rig checks that the states are declared and the names are not empty. rig tracker report sends the entry for the task's current state as the issue's status; a state with no entry sends no status (exit 1).

rig workflow validate reports each broken rule with its JSON path, for example tracker.map.priority.

0.3.0 cannot load a workflow file that has a tracker key, or a branch template that uses {key}. It rejects the unknown key or placeholder and exits 2. If one global file is shared between machines, update rig on all of them before you add either. Stores are not affected: 0.3.0 still reads a store that 0.4.0 wrote, and sees the current title and body of a linked task; it skips the events it does not know and shows a task made from an issue without its link or parent.

docs.title: Where the tracker is
docs.text:
These config keys (set with rig config) say which tracker and where:

Key Meaning tracker.kind local (no tracker, the default), jira, github, gitlab or exec. tracker.url The tracker's address, https:// only. Jira needs it; GitHub and GitLab need it only for a self-hosted server. tracker.project The Jira project key, or owner/name (group/.../name on GitLab). For GitHub and GitLab the default is the origin remote's path. tracker.command For exec: the program and its arguments, a list. Global file only. tracker.jira.api auto (default), v2 (Server or Data Center) or v3 (Cloud). tracker.jira.epicField The Server or Data Center "Epic Link" field id. Found by name when unset. tracker.jira.acceptanceField The id of the Jira field that holds acceptance criteria. Without it, an issue has none.

Trust. tracker.url decides where a login token is sent, so a repository cannot supply it. If .rig/config.json is tracked by git (or is a symlink, or rig cannot tell), rig ignores a tracker.url in it and the tracker commands stop with an error; rig tracker status still exits 0 and reports trusted: false. Set it in the global file or an untracked local file. tracker.command is a program rig would run, so it is read only from the global file.

GitHub and GitLab hosts. For github and gitlab rig takes the host from tracker.url. With no tracker.url, it takes the host from the origin remote, but only if that host is github.com (for GitHub), gitlab.com (for GitLab), or the host you named in forge.host. Any other host is refused, and the message says set tracker.url to the tracker's address. This is on purpose: a guessed host could read or link an issue on the wrong server.

docs.title: Linking, refreshing, unlinking
docs.text:
A task is unique by its link: one issue is linked from one task. The link is identified by the tracker kind, the host, the key and, for GitHub and GitLab, the project. Keys match whatever their case. Creating a task from an issue that is already linked (rig task new --from, rig tracker pull) returns the task that has it; rig task link on an issue another task has is refused (exit 1).

A worked example, with a GitHub repository:

rig config set tracker.kind github --repo        # use this repository's issues
rig tracker pull 42                               # make a task from issue 42
rig tracker pull --label ready --children        # make tasks from a label, and their sub-issues
rig tracker refresh --all                         # re-read every linked issue
rig tracker refresh --all --dry-run               # show what a refresh would change
rig task link 07 43                               # link the existing task 07 to issue 43
rig task unlink 07                                # drop the link; the fields stay

pull and task new --from copy the owned fields from the issue into a new task. refresh copies them again. The tracker wins: a refresh overwrites an owned field you edited locally, and lists it under replaced in --json with the value that was lost. A deleted issue is reported as gone and nothing is written. task unlink leaves the fields as they are; from then on they are the task's own.

docs.title: Worked example: a review loop
docs.text:
An example review workflow: plan, implement, review, verify, pull request, merge. It is one workflow among others. The file below is the fixture rig tests against (internal/workflow/testdata/review-loop.json); a project that uses it keeps its own copy.

{
  "name": "review-loop",
  "version": 1,
  "initial": "planned",
  "branch": "task/{short}-{slug}",
  "states": {
    "planned":      { "action": "implement" },
    "implementing": { "action": "review" },
    "reviewed":     { "action": "verify" },
    "verified":     { "action": "open-pr",  "shaBound": true },
    "pr_open":      { "action": "wait-ci",  "shaBound": true },
    "ci_green":     { "action": "mark-ready", "shaBound": true },
    "ready":        { "action": "merge", "who": "human", "shaBound": true },
    "merged":       { "final": true },
    "stopped":      { "action": "decide", "who": "human" }
  },
  "onNewCommit": "implementing",
  "transitions": [
    { "from": "planned", "to": "implementing",
      "gates": [{ "dependsIn": ["merged"] }] },
    { "from": "implementing", "to": "reviewed",
      "gates": [{ "noOpenFindings": { "severity": ["P1", "P2", "STYLE", "SPEC"] } }] },
    { "from": "reviewed", "to": "verified", "takes": "sha",
      "gates": [{ "shaIsHead": true }] },
    { "from": "reviewed", "to": "implementing", "count": "rounds",
      "gates": [{ "counterBelow": { "counter": "rounds", "max": 4 } }] },
    { "from": "verified", "to": "pr_open", "takes": "pr" },
    { "from": "pr_open", "to": "ci_green", "takes": "sha",
      "gates": [{ "shaIs": "verified" }] },
    { "from": "ci_green", "to": "ready" },
    { "from": "ready", "to": "merged", "takes": "sha" },
    { "from": ["verified", "pr_open", "ci_green", "ready"], "to": "implementing" },
    { "from": "*", "to": "stopped", "takes": "reason" },
    { "from": "stopped", "to": "$previous" }
  ],
  "fields": {
    "acceptance": { "type": "list", "context": true },
    "owns":       { "type": "paths", "context": true, "owns": true },
    "depends":    { "type": "tasks" }
  },
  "findings": {
    "severities": ["P1", "P2", "P3", "STYLE", "SPEC", "NOTE"],
    "fields": { "route": { "type": "enum", "values": ["implementer", "orchestrator"] } }
  },
  "counters": ["rounds"],
  "hooks": [
    { "on": "enter:stopped", "run": ["notify-user", "{short}", "{reason}"] }
  ]
}

Reading it through:

  • Starting. A task begins in planned. It cannot move to implementing until every task in its depends field is merged.
  • Review. implementing -> reviewed is refused while any P1, P2, STYLE or SPEC finding is open. P3 and NOTE findings never block.
  • Verifying. reviewed -> verified takes the sha that was reviewed and needs it to be the branch head. verified, pr_open, ci_green and ready are sha-bound, so a new commit on the branch drops the task back to implementing with no one having to notice. rig task is <t> verified answers "was this verified at the current head?" with one exit code.
  • Rounds. reviewed -> implementing is the only way back from reviewed. It counts a round and is refused once rounds reaches 4. The from-list of the plain -> implementing transition therefore leaves reviewed out: if it were there, the same route would exist twice, and validation would refuse the file, and the round cap could be skipped.
  • Pull request. verified -> pr_open records the pull request number and carries verified's sha. pr_open -> ci_green needs the sha it is given to be the one recorded at verified.
  • Merge. ready is for a human. ready -> merged is final.
  • Stopping. From any state but merged, a task can be stopped with a reason, which runs the notify-user hook. stopped -> $previous returns it to the state it left.

docs.title: When the workflow changes under a task
docs.text: A task records the workflow's name and version when it is created, but gates use the workflow loaded now. A task in a state the current workflow lacks is reported by rig workflow validate, and by rig next with the action unknown-state. A * transition can still move it.
